scenes.narration: [serious] In 1988, one student's test broke a tenth of the internet.
His name was Robert Morris. He studied at Cornell University. He wrote a program that could copy itself.
He said he only wanted to count how big the internet was. He let it go from MIT.
But there was one mistake. It copied itself too many times. Computers slowed down, then almost stopped.
In one day, about 6,000 of 60,000 computers were hit.
Then the FBI followed the trail back to his computer at Cornell.
In 1990, he was the first found guilty under a new U.S. law. No prison. Today he teaches at MIT.

facts.claim: The worm was launched on the evening of November 2, 1988 and crashed about 6,000 Unix machines, roughly 10% of the internet at the time

Robert Morris was a Cornell computer science graduate student; about 6,000 of roughly 60,000 internet-connected machines were affected within 24 hours; the FBI traced it to his Cornell machine although it first seemed to come from MIT
Morris said the worm was designed to gauge the size of the internet; he released it by hacking into an MIT computer from his Cornell terminal; a programming error caused major slowdowns

Morris was the first person convicted under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (convicted 1990) and received three years' probation, 400 hours of community service and a $10,050 fine, with no prison time
Morris later earned a PhD at Harvard and has taught at MIT since the mid-2000s

seo.title: Morris Worm: The 1988 Experiment That Crashed the Internet
seo.description: In 1988 a Cornell graduate student released a self-copying program to measure the internet. A mistake made it spread out of control and hit about 6,000 machines. Learn how the Morris worm of 1988 crashed early internet computers. #cybersecurity #morrisworm #techhistory #shorts
